task: You support an airline network operations team after complaints about late and cancelled flights rose over the winter. Leadership wants to know where unreliability concentrates before choosing where to act: how reliable U.S. domestic flying was in January–March 2025, which airlines and airports were weakest, and what causes most delay.

produce.name: Network baseline
produce.about: Scheduled, cancelled and diverted flights, with the cancellation rate, on-time rate and average delay.

produce.name: Airline comparison
produce.about: Flights, cancellation rate and on-time rate for each airline.

produce.name: Delay causes
produce.about: Delay minutes and share for each of the five causes.

produce.name: Airport list
produce.about: The ten busy origin airports with the highest cancellation rate.

produce.name: Reliability assessment
produce.about: Three findings and one operational recommendation.

summaries.understand-data: Compare a cancelled and a delayed flight and see which columns are filled.
summaries.baseline: Measure the network's cancellation rate, on-time rate and average delay.
summaries.airlines: Compare airlines by cancellation and on-time rates.
summaries.causes: Split the delay minutes of late flights across the five causes.
summaries.airports: Rank busy origin airports by cancellation rate.
summaries.synthesis: Decide where operations should act first, separating causes airlines control from those they don't.
summaries.report: Write three findings and one operational recommendation.

problems: Cancelled and diverted flights have no arrival delay at all: it is missing, not zero.
The five delay-cause columns are filled only for flights that arrived 15 or more minutes late.
Early arrivals are stored as negative delays, and most flights arrive early.
Airlines fly very different volumes, from about 1,500 to over 24,000 flights, so raw counts mislead.
Most origin airports have fewer than 1,000 departures, where a few cancellations swing the rate.
